security_audit.summary: Static command findings are false positives caused by Markdown code fences, inline backticks, and SDK examples rather than shell execution. The hardcoded URLs are Azure Queue Storage placeholders, not covert network destinations. No prompt injection or malicious exfiltration intent was found, but the documentation should improve dependency pinning and avoid printing queue payloads.

remediation.suggestion: Recommend pinned package versions, supported version ranges, or a constraints file for azure-storage-queue and azure-identity.

remediation.issue: Queue payloads printed in sample receive flows
remediation.suggestion: Show redacted logging or metadata-only output instead of printing full message.content in examples.

content.user_title: Manage Azure Queue Storage with Python
content.value_statement: Python teams need reliable patterns for queue-based background work in Azure. This skill provides focused SDK examples for creating queues, sending messages, receiving work, and handling async processing.
actual_capabilities: Shows how to install azure-storage-queue and azure-identity for Python projects.
Demonstrates DefaultAzureCredential authentication with QueueServiceClient and QueueClient.
Covers queue creation, deletion, listing, metadata, and property inspection.
Explains sending, receiving, peeking, updating, deleting, and clearing queue messages.
Includes async QueueClient usage for high-throughput processing patterns.
Shows BinaryBase64EncodePolicy and BinaryBase64DecodePolicy for binary message content.
limitations: It is a reference guide, not a runnable project or test suite.
It does not cover Azure role assignment, account provisioning, or local emulator setup.
It does not include retry policy tuning, observability, or production deployment templates.
It uses placeholder account URLs and example queue names that users must replace.

use_cases.title: Add Queue Processing to a Python Service
use_cases.description: Use the SDK examples to add send and receive flows for background jobs in an Azure-hosted service.

use_cases.title: Review Azure Queue Operations
use_cases.description: Check common queue operations before writing scripts that create queues, inspect metadata, or clear old messages.

use_cases.title: Plan Async Message Workers
use_cases.description: Use the async client example to design workers that receive messages and delete them after processing.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Basic Queue Client
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for a new Python project
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to show the steps for creating an Azure Queue Storage client in Python with DefaultAzureCredential.

prompt_templates.title: Send and Receive Work Items
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to outline a Python flow that sends task messages, receives them with a visibility timeout, and deletes them after processing.

prompt_templates.title: Handle Poison Message Detection
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to explain how dequeue_count and visibility_timeout can help identify messages that repeatedly fail processing.

prompt_templates.title: Design an Async Queue Worker
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to design an async Python worker pattern for Azure Queue Storage, including send, receive, delete, and Base64 handling for binary content.

output_examples.input: Ask for a basic Azure Queue Storage setup in Python.
output_examples.output: The response explains package installation, DefaultAzureCredential, account URL configuration, and creating QueueServiceClient and QueueClient objects.

output_examples.input: Ask how to process messages safely after receiving them.
output_examples.output: The response describes receiving messages with a visibility timeout, processing each item, deleting successful messages, and checking dequeue counts for repeated failures.

output_examples.input: Ask whether the skill covers async queue access.
output_examples.output: The response summarizes the async QueueClient pattern, including async context management, receiving messages, and deleting processed messages.

best_practices: Use managed identity or DefaultAzureCredential instead of embedding storage credentials in prompts or code.
Set visibility timeout and time to live values based on real processing and retry requirements.
Delete messages only after successful processing and monitor dequeue counts for repeated failures.
anti_patterns: Do not copy placeholder account URLs or queue names into production without replacing them.
Do not print full message contents when queues may contain secrets or customer data.
Do not clear queues unless the operation is reviewed and expected by the application owner.

faq.question: Does this skill create Azure resources automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides Python SDK guidance and examples. Users must run commands and code in their own Azure environment.

faq.question: Which Python package does it focus on?
faq.answer: It focuses on azure-storage-queue and uses azure-identity for DefaultAzureCredential authentication.

faq.question: Does it support async queue processing?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes an async QueueClient example using azure.storage.queue.aio and azure.identity.aio.

faq.question: Can it help with binary message content?
faq.answer: Yes. It shows Azure Queue Storage Base64 encode and decode policies for binary data.

faq.question: Does it cover Azure Service Bus?
faq.answer: No. It only mentions Service Bus as an option for advanced features such as sessions and topics.

faq.question: Is it suitable for production security design?
faq.answer: It is a starting reference. Production systems still need access control, monitoring, retry policies, and secret-handling review.
